1191.title: The Risalah
1191.hook: his book laid out the method of law, founding usul al-fiqh
1191.howItsDone: Students of Islamic law study usul al-fiqh, the roots of law, alongside the rulings themselves, and al-Shafi'i's Risalah is read as a foundational work in that field.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Imam al-Shafi'i, student of Malik and reader of the Hanafis. Your line: learned from both.

It begins as a letter. A hadith scholar in Basra, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, writes to al-Shafi'i with a request, as the story is told: write me something on how the Qur'an is to be understood, on when a report is to be accepted, on consensus, and on how one text can replace another. Explain how it all fits. Al-Shafi'i answers, and the answer grows into a book. It keeps the plain name of what it was: al-Risalah, the letter. With it, scholars had a shared page on which to argue over method, not only over rulings.
screen: `A REQUEST FROM BASRA.` → `HOW DOES IT ALL FIT?` → `THE ANSWER BECOMES A BOOK.`

segments.voice: These last two weeks showed Kufa's careful judgment and Medina's living practice, each strong, each sure of itself. Al-Shafi'i asked something prior: before any ruling, how do we know where to look, and in what order? That's usul al-fiqh, the roots of law, and tradition remembers the Risalah as the book where that discipline begins. The order he set: the Qur'an first. Then the sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, which al-Shafi'i argued explains the Qur'an and must be followed, even when it comes through a single reliable narrator. That pushed against Medina's practice, where the city could outweigh a lone report. Then consensus. Then analogy, qiyas, measured carefully from a text. Then a method for language. A verse can sound general and still be meant more narrowly. One text can explain another. When two reports seem to clash, his first move is to look for a way both are true before setting either aside. And the argument from Abu Hanifa's school: in the Risalah he rejects istihsan where it isn't tied to a text, calling it a jurist pleasing himself. The Hanafis kept arguing back. Some readers say that even then, the argument ran in his terms: what is your source, and what is your step? Not the answer first. Method first.
screen: `USUL AL-FIQH: THE ROOTS OF LAW.` · `QUR'AN, SUNNAH, CONSENSUS, ANALOGY.` · `TWO REPORTS CLASH: SEEK BOTH TRUE.` · `WHAT IS YOUR SOURCE, YOUR STEP?`

segments.voice: Here's one principle al-Shafi'i works through: the Qur'an gives children shares in their parents' estate in general terms, a report in Jami' al-Tirmidhi says a killer does not inherit, and the general rule stands while the specific one narrows it. Now take a broad rule you keep, like always answering the phone for family, and name a specific exception you already live by. Notice how the two fit together instead of fighting, and if you pray, ask for clear understanding.
The Risalah. Al-Shafi'i's letter that grew into a book, setting out how law is to be found: its sources, their order, and how texts explain each other. Today's word.
Your line: method first. Before you argue over an answer, ask where to look. Until tomorrow.

1192.title: His poems
1192.hook: al-Shafi'i also wrote poetry on travel, knowledge and patience
1192.howItsDone: Verses attributed to al-Shafi'i, gathered in a collection called his Diwan, are read and memorized by students of Islamic learning, especially the lines on travel, memory and patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Risalah, al-Shafi'i's letter that became a book of method. Your line: method first.

Water that sits still goes bad. Water that runs stays sweet. That line doesn't come from a law book. It comes from a poem, and tradition puts it in the mouth of the man who wrote the Risalah. Al-Shafi'i, the jurist who built rules for reading rules, also left verses, or verses gathered under his name: on leaving home, on learning, on waiting out hard days. They're short, plain, and easy to learn by heart. Today, the jurist as a poet.
screen: `STILL WATER GOES BAD.` → `RUNNING WATER STAYS SWEET.` → `THE JURIST AS A POET.`

segments.voice: The collection is called the Diwan of al-Shafi'i. Some readers doubt that every line in it is really his, so, honestly: lines told in his name. Three themes run through them. First, travel. One poem tells the reader to leave home in search of learning and honor: travel, and you'll find something to replace whatever you left behind. Then the pictures. Still water spoils; running water stays sweet. A lion that never leaves its den never hunts. An arrow that never leaves the bow never hits. Even the sun, if it stood still in the sky forever, people would grow tired of it. Second, knowledge. In a short pair of lines, the poet complains to his teacher Waki' about his poor memory. Waki' tells him to leave sins, because knowledge is a light, and the light of God is not given to one who sins. Study, for him, isn't only hours at a desk; how you live shapes what you can hold. Third, patience. Another poem opens by letting the days do whatever they will, and staying calm when the decree comes down. Hard times pass and good times pass; neither one stays. Together they give a portrait the law books don't: the man who argued line by line about evidence also left home, struggled to remember, and told himself to wait out bad days. Medina with Malik, then Iraq, then Egypt. He did what the poem says.
screen: `THE DIWAN: LINES TOLD IN HIS NAME.` · `TRAVEL: THE LION, THE ARROW, THE SUN.` · `KNOWLEDGE IS A LIGHT.` · `PATIENCE: LET THE DAYS DO AS THEY WILL.`

segments.voice: Say one line from the travel poem slowly, once: travel, and you'll find something to replace what you leave behind. Then ask where in your life the water has gone still, a routine, a room, a habit of thought, and what small travel might stir it: a different route home, a new book, a question for someone you don't usually ask. If you pray, you can ask for a journey that leads somewhere good.

1193.title: Egypt to Indonesia
1193.hook: the school is followed in Egypt, East Africa, Yemen and Southeast Asia
1193.howItsDone: Muslims in Egypt, East Africa, Yemen, parts of southern India and Southeast Asia commonly follow the Shafi'i school, and its manuals are studied in their mosques, schools and seminaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: his poems, al-Shafi'i's lines on travel, knowledge and patience. Your line: travel, and find.

A sail fills with a wind that keeps a calendar. For part of the year it blows one way across the Indian Ocean. Then the season turns, and so does the wind. Sailors timed their lives by it. They loaded cloth and spices and letters, and alongside the cargo they carried people who knew the law. Yesterday's poem said: travel, and you'll find. The school of al-Shafi'i traveled farther than he ever did. Today, where it went, and what carried it.
screen: `A WIND THAT KEEPS A CALENDAR.` → `CARGO, AND PEOPLE WHO KNEW THE LAW.` → `WHERE THE SCHOOL WENT.`

segments.voice: Start where he ended. Al-Shafi'i spent his last years in Egypt, and his tomb in Cairo still receives visitors. His students there kept his teaching, and from there it spread. The school is followed in Egypt, along the coast of East Africa, in Yemen, across Southeast Asia in places like Malaysia and Indonesia, and in parts of southern India, like Kerala. On a map, that's a shape of coastlines: many of these lands ring the Indian Ocean. Much of it went by sea, and by the wind. The monsoon blows across that water one way for part of the year, then turns back. Merchants from Arabia and Yemen sailed with it to the Swahili coast, to India, to the islands. They traded, married, settled, built mosques. Some were scholars; families of teachers from Hadramawt, in Yemen, became known for teaching far from home. When someone in a port town asked how to pray or how to divide an inheritance, the answer came out of the books these travelers carried. The Qur'an points at this kind of traffic. Among God's signs, it says, are the winds he sends as heralds of his mercy, so that ships may sail at his command and people may seek his bounty, and perhaps be thankful. A trade wind is an ordinary thing; in that verse, it's a sign. And the books are still read. In a village school in Java and a mosque on the Kenyan coast, students study manuals of the same school, such as the Minhaj of al-Nawawi. Far apart, the same pages, joined by water.
screen: `FROM HIS TOMB IN CAIRO.` · `A SHAPE OF COASTLINES.` · `CARRIED BY TRADERS ON THE MONSOON.` · `THE WINDS AS A SIGN.`

segments.voice: Picture the Indian Ocean, or open a map, and rest a finger in the middle of the water. Let your eyes travel slowly around the rim, one breath for each stretch: the Red Sea, the coast of Yemen, East Africa, southern India, the islands to the east, everything facing the same water and waiting on the same wind. If you pray, you can remember the travelers who carried what they knew.
Egypt to Indonesia. The lands of the Shafi'i school, strung around the Indian Ocean, linked by trade and by the monsoon. Today's word.

1194.title: Ahmad ibn Hanbal
1194.howItsDone: Hanbali scholars look first to the Qur'an and the hadith, then to the sayings of the Companions, and the school's rulings grew from Ahmad ibn Hanbal's recorded answers to questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Shafi'i school, from Egypt to Indonesia. Your line: by the monsoon.

An old man walks through Baghdad carrying an inkwell. Someone stops him. You've reached this rank, people call you an imam, and you still carry ink around like a student? His answer, in a saying reported of him: with the inkwell, to the grave. That's Ahmad ibn Hanbal: old, honored, and still copying the reports line by line. Today the Hanbali school begins, with a man who never stopped writing things down.
screen: `AN OLD MAN WITH AN INKWELL.` → `WITH THE INKWELL, TO THE GRAVE.` → `THE HANBALI SCHOOL BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Ahmad ibn Hanbal was a scholar of Baghdad, and above everything a scholar of hadith, the reports of what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said and did. He traveled for them, his biographers say, to Kufa and Basra, to Mecca and Medina, and as far as Yemen, hearing reports from the people who carried them and writing them down. He also studied with al-Shafi'i, and reports say each held the other in high regard. His method was his own. When a question came, he looked first to the Qur'an and the reports, then to what the Companions had said. And reports say he would rather act on a weak hadith than on a jurist's analogy, as long as nothing stronger stood against it. Weak, here, doesn't mean made up. It means a chain of narrators with some doubt in it. For him, a report with some doubt was still closer to the Prophet than a clever argument. Some early writers even listed him among the scholars of hadith rather than the jurists. His students saw it differently. They wrote down his answers, one by one, about prayer, trade, marriage and manners, and out of those answers his school was built. So his law is a law of answers: ask him something, and the reply might be a report, passed on rather than argued.
screen: `A SCHOLAR WHO TRAVELED FOR REPORTS.` · `A WEAK REPORT OVER A CLEVER ANALOGY.` · `A LAW OF ANSWERS.` · `AND KEEP CARRYING THE INK.`

segments.voice: Here's a short hadith, the one that opens Sahih al-Bukhari: actions are only by intentions, in Arabic innamal a'malu bin-niyyat. Say it three times slowly, in whichever language sits easier, then once with your eyes closed, and ask what intention sits under the next thing you'll do today. If you pray, you can ask that your intentions be good ones; if not, just keep the line on your tongue.

1195.title: The Musnad
1195.hook: his vast collection of reports, arranged by Companion
1195.howItsDone: Students of hadith consult Ahmad ibn Hanbal's Musnad by looking up the Companion who narrated a report, and modern printed editions often add scholars' grades beside its reports.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the scholar with the inkwell. Your line: the imam of hadith.

There are two ways to shelve a library of sayings. By subject: everything on prayer here, everything on fasting there, trade in the next room. Or by who told you: every story your grandmother told on one shelf, every story your uncle told on the next. Sahih al-Bukhari, whose opening report was yesterday's practice, takes the first way. Ahmad ibn Hanbal's great book takes the second. Today, the book, and why the shelving matters.
screen: `TWO WAYS TO SHELVE A LIBRARY.` → `BY SUBJECT, OR BY WHO TOLD YOU.` → `AHMAD CHOSE THE SECOND.`

segments.voice: Its name is the Musnad. A musnad report has its chain of narrators attached, leaning back link by link to the Prophet. A book called a Musnad is arranged by Companion, the person who heard the Prophet. Open it and you find the reports of Abu Bakr together, then those of 'Umar, and on through the Companions, men and women, each with a section of their own. A reader hunting one topic has to search; a reader who wants one Companion's voice finds it all in one place. It is vast. His biographers say he gathered it across a lifetime, choosing it from the far larger body of reports he had heard, and meant it as a reference when people disagreed over a sunnah. His son 'Abd Allah is reported to have heard it from him and passed it on, adding reports of his own. Because Ahmad included reports he judged usable, not only the strongest, strong and weaker reports sit side by side. Later scholars graded them one by one, and some modern editions print a grade beside each. So the Musnad isn't a law book, or a book of only the strongest hadith. It's a storehouse. Some of its reports appear in other collections too. Here's one, told by the Companion Anas ibn Malik: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. It's in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, and in the Musnad it sits on the shelf of the one who told it.
screen: `MUSNAD: ARRANGED BY COMPANION.` · `GATHERED ACROSS A LIFETIME.` · `STRONG AND WEAKER, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `A STOREHOUSE, SHELVED BY VOICE.`

Hold their name for a few breaths, and if you pray, you can ask for it for them.

1196.title: The trial
1196.hook: he was flogged for refusing a state doctrine that the Qur'an was created
1196.howItsDone: Hanbali scholars and students tell the story of Ahmad ibn Hanbal's trial as an example of steadfastness, and Sunni creeds state that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Musnad, hadith shelved by Companion. Your line: a vast collection.

A room in the caliph's palace, and a man in chains. The question put to him is short: is the Qur'an created? Say yes, and you go home. Judges have said yes. Other scholars, under pressure, have said yes. He won't. He asks his questioners for a verse of the Qur'an, or a word from the Prophet, that says it. They don't give him one he accepts. So the whips come out. The man is Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the collector from yesterday, and the ordeal has a name.
screen: `A MAN IN CHAINS, ONE QUESTION.` → `SAY YES, AND GO HOME.` → `HE WON'T.`

segments.voice: The name is the mihnah: the trial, the ordeal. It began under the caliph al-Ma'mun. His court had taken up a position held by theologians called the Mu'tazila: that the Qur'an, as God's speech, was created, not eternal with God. They held it, as they understood it, to protect God's oneness: if the Qur'an is eternal alongside God, aren't there two eternal things? Ahmad and the hadith scholars around him held the opposite: the Qur'an is the speech of God, and God's speech is not a created thing. The caliph ordered judges and scholars questioned. One after another, people gave way. Ahmad refused. He was imprisoned, and under the next caliph, al-Mu'tasim, he was flogged. The reports keep returning to one reply: give me something from the Book of God or the sunnah of His Messenger, and I'll say it. He wasn't trying to win a philosophy debate on the court's terms. He was refusing to make the texts say something he didn't find in them. In the end he was released, and later, under another caliph, the mihnah ended. The Qur'an speaks of testing too: God will try people with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops, and gives good news to those who are patient. To be fair to both sides: the Mu'tazila saw themselves defending God's unity, and Ahmad saw himself defending the text. Muslim theologians still study both arguments. What the story keeps, especially in the Hanbali school, is one scholar who would not say it.

1197.hook: the Hanbali school is followed mainly in Saudi Arabia and Qatar
1197.howItsDone: In Saudi Arabia and Qatar the Hanbali school shapes courts, mosques and teaching, and its manuals, including Ibn Qudamah's al-Mughni, are studied and consulted by scholars of other schools as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mihnah, and the scholar who would not bend under it. Your line: he would not say it.

It's the smallest of the Sunni schools by number of followers. And yet people describe it with a second word too: steadfast. How does one school earn both names? The answer runs through Baghdad and Damascus, a large book that makes room for the other schools, and the trial one man would not bend under. Today, the end of the Hanbali story: where it's followed now.

segments.voice: Today the Hanbali school is followed mainly in Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It's described as the smallest of the Sunni schools by number of followers, which is where the first half of today's line comes from. But size isn't the whole story. For a long time its home was Baghdad, where Ahmad taught and was buried, and later Damascus, where Hanbali scholars ran their own circles. One of them, Ibn Qudamah, wrote a large book of law called al-Mughni. Question by question, it lays out the other schools' views beside the Hanbali one, with their evidence, and students of other schools consult it too. A book from the smallest school that makes room for everyone's arguments. Now, steadfast. The school carries the memory of yesterday's trial. Its method stays close to the texts: the Qur'an, the hadith, the sayings of the Companions, with caution about reasoning that runs out ahead of them. The next part may surprise you. In everyday trade, Hanbali jurists are known for a wide view of contracts: the deals and conditions people agree to are permitted unless a text forbids them. So the school known for holding close to the texts also leaves wide room where the texts are silent. Holding firm on what is written, and not inventing walls where nothing is written: both come from the same respect for the text. And smallest names a size, not a rank. This path doesn't rank the schools. Each has its lands, its books, its memory.
